about: Data pilot, 20 November 2026. Positions come from Otis's report of 1899 (the telegrams and their clock times), the January 1899 roster of the Eighth Army Corps, and the Signal Corps map of February 1899 with its index of final positions. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.

The Filipino side is thin: the sources read are American, and Taylor's notes on the Filipino commands around Manila date from August-September 1898. Every Filipino position is inferred, and the commanders named are those of 1898.
Many clock times are ranges: the reports give "early in the morning" or "during the afternoon". Telegram times (11:20, 12:30, about 16:30, 16:45) are exact to the minute.
The 1899 map is a blue-line photocopy drawn with north to the left, shown turned to north-up and fitted to today's ground to within about 170 m (at worst 270 m).
Symbols are blue for the Americans and red for the Filipino army; the colours are a drawing convention.

Ships are drawn where the reports read have them firing in support of the troops, landing men or carrying them. Their places on the water are estimates (the reports say "off" a town and no more), and this is the Army's account: no naval report was read.

opening.label: Before 20:30
opening.text: Evening of 4 February 1899. The Eighth Army Corps holds a line of blockhouses around Manila, with the Filipino army entrenched facing it. Press play: the first shot is fired at Santa Mesa at 20:30.

units.name: Army of the Philippine Republic about Manila
units.label: Ricarte (Aug 1898)
units.notes: Taylor (S67) puts Gen. Artemio Ricarte "in command of entire insurgent army about Manila" in August 1898 and says the failure of the attack of 4-5 Feb "greatly impaired his prestige". Who commanded on 4 Feb 1899 is not stated in the sources read. Strength not in the sources read.

assignments.notes: Dated by Taylor to August 1898. Not shown for February 1899.

units.name: Third zone of Manila (Col. Luciano San Miguel)
units.label: 3rd zone (San Miguel)
units.notes: Taylor (S67): "Col. San Miguel. It was in this zone that outbreak of February 4 occurred." Echelon "brigade" is a drawing choice for a zone command; its size is not in the sources read.

assignments.notes: Taylor names San Miguel as chief of the 3rd zone (Aug 1898) and puts the outbreak of 4 Feb in this zone; the dates of his command are not given.

units.name: Fourth zone, Caloocan
units.label: 4th zone (Caloocan)
units.notes: Taylor (S67): Lt. Col. Pilar "commanding 4th zone, Caloocan", 22 Aug 1898; Pantaleon Garcia "at this time in command at Caloocan" (Aug 1898). Who held it on 4 Feb 1899 is not in the sources read.

units.name: Filipino forces south of Manila (Pineda/Pasay)
units.label: South of Manila
units.notes: Taylor (S67): Gen. Mariano Noriel "in command of insurgents south of Manila", July-Aug 1898, at Pineda (Pasay) and Paranaque. Not shown to be his on 4 Feb 1899.

units.name: Filipino forces at San Pedro Macati
units.label: S. Pedro Macati
units.notes: Taylor (S67): Gen. Pio del Pilar at San Pedro Macati, Aug 1898; his command "extended to meet that of Noriel, at Pineda". Not shown to be his on 4 Feb 1899.

events.name: First shot at Santa Mesa
events.label: First shot
events.text: A Nebraska picket near Santa Mesa fires on a Filipino soldier who will not halt, and the lines open fire. The battle begins at 20:30.

events.name: Firing along the north front through the night
events.label: Night firing
events.text: Fire is exchanged along the north front from the Pasig to the Lico road; heavy at midnight and at 04:00. South of the Pasig, Anderson is told to hold and not attack.

events.name: Anderson allowed to attack
events.label: South attacks
events.text: Anderson's division south of the Pasig is allowed to attack. King swings his brigade left towards the Pasig.

events.name: Stotsenburg takes Blockhouses 6 and 7
events.label: Blockhouses 6 and 7
events.text: The 1st Nebraska attacks at first light and takes Blockhouses 6 and 7.

events.name: Nebraskans cross the San Juan bridge
events.label: San Juan bridge
events.text: The Nebraskans cross the San Juan River at the bridge and take the powder magazine and the reservoir, El Deposito.

events.name: King takes Santa Ana
events.label: Santa Ana
events.text: King's brigade takes Santa Ana; many Filipinos drown trying to cross the Pasig. The Californians enter San Pedro Macati.

events.name: Ovenshine takes Pasay
events.label: Pasay
events.text: Ovenshine swings left, clears the ground in front of the centre and takes Pasay without resistance.

events.name: Close of the day
events.label: Evening line
events.text: The battle ends about 17:00. The Americans hold the road from Pasay to San Pedro Macati in the south, and the reservoir, San Juan del Monte and the blockhouses in the north.

Fitted to the ground on nine places that still stand (churches, the Walled City's south bastion, Paco cemetery, Malacanang): places on it fall within about 170 m of where they are, at worst 270 m. "Former ... outpost" labels are positions before the battle; the heavy double-dashed lines named for regiments are their final positions, after the capture of Caloocan on 10 Feb. South of the city this sketch is not to scale: placed on the ground with the rest of the sheet, its Pasay falls 1.3 km south-east of Pasay. The reconstructed map shows them on the right ground.

reconstructions.title: Manila and vicinity, February 1899: a WarMapper reconstruction
reconstructions.label: 1899 (reconstructed)
reconstructions.about: This is a WarMapper reconstruction, not a period map. It is drawn by this page, live, from lines read off two Army maps of February 1899 and, south of Malate, a War Department plan of 1898, in the manner of a map of the time. The shore is the shore of 1899: most of today's bay front was reclaimed later. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.
reconstructions.note: Proof of concept. North of the Pasig and in the city the lines come from the engineer map (S78), tied to today's ground to about 20-30 m (weaker at Caloocan). From Malate to Pasay the shore, Calle Real, blockhouses 13 and 14 and the plan's own lines come from the War Department plan of 1898 (S79), slid to today's streets and good to about 100 m; that is the ground of 1898. South of Pasay, and the Pasig above Santa Ana, are still from the Signal Corps map (S64) and may be 200-400 m out. Second pass, 21 Nov 2026: the engineer map's own street, block, dyke and field lines and its esteros were added by program. They give the city and the country their detail, but nobody has checked them line by line.
reconstructions.credit: WarMapper reconstruction from Haan, 1899 (National Archives), "Manila y sus arrabales", 1898 (Yale) and Warking, 1899 (Library of Congress)

features.desc: Roads, field lines, marsh and old works: Malate, Singalong and the strip to Pasay
features.basis: Every dark ink line of the 1898 sheet south of where the engineer map stops, separated from the scan by a program, thinned and vectorised, then placed as the shore of this layer's map is. It holds roads, field lines, the estero and marsh behind Malate, the old Spanish line of works by blockhouses 13 and 14, and the trenches the Americans dug in August 1898. Nobody has checked it line by line, and it is the ground of 1898, six months before the battle.

features.name: Calle Real
features.desc: Calle Real from the fort at Malate to the road to Pasay church
features.basis: Read from crops of "Manila y sus arrabales" (War Department, 1898; 4,551 x 7,118 scan) and checked by laying the picks back on the scan. Placed by that sheet's fit to the engineer map; south of Malate, where the sheet is a hand-drawn strip, slid to today's F. B. Harrison Street crossings as well (pipeline/georef/manila_arrabales_fit.py). The shore is that of 1898. The road drawn as a double line nearest the shore; the sheet letters it "Calle Real" in Malate.
